theoryAdd.text: Going Deeper: Static, const, this and Friends

A class body only describes a type, and the same class definition is normally included into many source files, so the declaration static int count; inside it cannot reserve storage without creating one copy per file. The out-of-class definition int Counter::count = 0; written in exactly one .cpp file is where the single shared object is actually created, and the linker connects every use of Counter::count to it. Static data members have static storage duration: they exist before main() starts, are zero-initialised when no initialiser is written, and live until the program ends. Integral static const members and static constexpr members may be initialised inside the class, and C++17 also allows inline static int count = 0; which needs no separate definition.

theoryAdd.plainText: sizeof(T) = sum of the sizes of the non-static data members + padding; static members and member functions add nothing

theoryAdd.text:
Worked example 1 - output: 2 1
T a, b;      default constructor runs twice            n = 2
f(a);        x is built by the implicit copy
             constructor, which does not do ++n        n = 2
             f prints T::n                              "2 "
             x is destroyed when the call ends: --n      n = 1
cout << T::n                                            "1"
Two objects (a and b) are alive, yet n says 1.
Fix: add T(const T &) { ++n; }  ->  the output becomes 3 2

Worked example 2 - output: 60
Arr x;          d = {4, 5, 6}
x.at(1) = 50;   x is non-const, so int& at(int) is chosen: d[1] = 50
total(x)        a is a const Arr&, so int at(int) const is chosen
                a.at(0) + a.at(1) + a.at(2) = 4 + 50 + 6 = 60
Without the const overload total() would not compile, because a
const object (or const reference) may call only const member functions.

theoryAdd.text: The compiler implements a member call obj.f(a) by passing &obj as a hidden first argument named this. Inside a non-const member function this has type T*, and inside a const member function it has type const T*, which is exactly why a const function can neither assign to ordinary members nor call non-const member functions. A static member function is called without any object, so no hidden argument exists; that is also why a static function cannot be const, volatile or virtual, since all three describe the object behind this. A friend function is an ordinary non-member even when its body is written inside the class, so it has no this either and must name the object it uses, as in v.x.
Mistakes that cost marks in this topic:
items: Repeating static in the out-of-class definition (static int Counter::count = 0;) is a compile error; the keyword belongs only on the declaration inside the class.
Dropping const from the out-of-class definition of a const member function: int T::get() { ... } does not match the declaration int get() const; and does not compile.
Counting objects in the constructor and destructor but not in the copy constructor, so copies are destroyed without ever having been counted.
Returning the object by value (T f() { ...; return *this; }) when chaining is intended: every later call in the chain changes a temporary copy.
Defining a friend function with a class prefix (void T::show(...)): a friend is not a member, so the compiler looks for a member that does not exist.
Returning int& to a data member from a const member function: the member is const there, so only const int& or a copy may be returned.

theoryAdd.text: For output questions on static counters, list every creation in order (plain objects, array elements, new, copies made by pass-by-value or T b = a, and static locals) and every destruction (end of block, delete, end of function). A static local object is constructed only on the first call of its function, and a counting constructor is skipped whenever the compiler-generated copy constructor is used.

Put int Counter::count = 0; in exactly one .cpp file, never in a header that several files include: each inclusion creates another definition and the linker reports a multiple-definition error. In C++17 the alternative is to write inline static int count = 0; inside the class.

questions.questionText: Class Cls declares static int count; inside its body. Which line, written once outside the class, correctly defines this static data member?
questions.explanation: The definition names the member with the class qualifier and must not repeat static: int Cls::count = 0;. Writing static there is a compile error, and int count = 0; merely creates an unrelated global variable, leaving Cls::count undefined at link time.

options: It compiles, but linking fails with an undefined reference to Counter::n
Compile error: a static data member must be initialised inside the class
questions.explanation: static int n; inside the class is only a declaration; without the out-of-class definition int Counter::n = 0; no storage exists, so every source line compiles but the linker cannot resolve Counter::n.

options: Compile error: a static member needs an initialiser
Link error: undefined reference to C::k
questions.explanation: int C::k; and double C::r; are valid definitions without initialisers. Static data members have static storage duration, so they are zero-initialised before main() runs and the program prints 0 0.
Only the non-static members a and c live inside each object: sizeof(S) = 4 + 4 = 8. The static b and the member function take no space in objects, so sizeof(x) + sizeof(y) = 8 + 8 = 16.

questions.questionText: Class Item has a public data member declared static int count;. Which statement about count is NOT correct?
options: It can be used as Item::count even before any Item object exists
It exists for the whole run of the program, like a global variable
It can also be reached through an object, as obj.count
Every Item object holds its own copy of count, so sizeof(Item) grows by sizeof(count)
questions.explanation: A static data member is stored once, outside all objects, so it does not add to sizeof(Item) and is not copied per object. The other three statements are true: it is reachable through the class name or any object and has static storage duration.
next++ hands out the current value and then increments the shared counter, so a, b and c get ids 100, 101 and 102. a.get() + c.get() = 100 + 102 = 202 and b.get() = 101.

a and c use T() (n = 2), but T b = a uses the compiler-generated copy constructor, which does not change n, so 2 is printed. At the closing brace both c and b run ~T(), giving n = 2 - 2 = 0 even though a is still alive.

questions.questionText: In C++17, which of these declarations written inside a class body is a compile error?
questions.explanation: A non-const, non-inline static data member may not have an initialiser inside the class; it must be defined outside as int X::count = 0;. Integral static const members, static constexpr members and C++17 inline static members may all be initialised in the class.

questions.questionText: Class Util has the public member function static int sq(int x) { return x * x; }. Which expression calls it correctly when no Util object exists?
questions.explanation: A static member function belongs to the class, so it is called with the scope resolution operator: Util::sq(4). The dot and arrow operators need an object or a pointer, and plain sq(4) is not in scope outside the class.

questions.questionText: Inside the body of a static member function, which members of its class can be named directly?
options: only the non-static data members of the object it is called through
every data member of the class, reached through the this pointer
only the public members of the class, whether static or not
only the static members of the class, plus its own parameters and locals
questions.explanation: A static member function is not called on an object, so it has no this pointer and cannot name non-static members directly. It may use the class's static members (public or private) and anything passed to it as arguments.
g() is static and therefore has no this pointer, so it cannot use the non-static member a. A static function may use static b and call static f(), and the ordinary member h() may use both a and b.
Calling a static function through p, through q or through K:: makes no difference: all three calls update the single shared v. v = 5 + 3 + 4 + 1 = 13.

questions.questionText: Why can a static member function not be declared const, as in static int f() const;?
options: Because static functions must always return void
Because a const member function must also be virtual
Because const after the parameter list makes the object pointed to by this const, and a static function has no this pointer
Because static functions are stored in read-only memory
questions.explanation: The trailing const qualifies the implicit object (this becomes const T*). A static member function is called without an object and receives no this, so there is nothing for const to apply to and the compiler rejects the declaration.
The static local s is constructed only on the first call of make(), while the ordinary local t is constructed on every call. Constructions: 1 (s) + 3 (t) = 4.
A derived class shares its base's static member, so P::c and Q::c are the same variable. a adds 1; each Q object first runs P() (+1) and then Q() (+10): c = 1 + 11 + 11 = 23, printed twice.

questions.questionText: Which declaration inside class Box makes show() a constant member function, one that can be called on a const Box object?
questions.explanation: The keyword const goes after the parameter list: void show() const;. const before the return type only qualifies the (void) result, void show(const) is a syntax error, and static void show(); declares a static function, which has no this pointer and so is not a const member function.

a is a const object, so it may call only const member functions. a.get() is const and fine in Lines A and B, and b is non-const so b.set() is allowed, but a.set(9) calls a non-const function on a const object.

questions.questionText: Class T has the data member int x;. Which member function defined inside T fails to compile?
options: int g() const { x++; return x; }
int h() const { int y = x; y++; return y; }
questions.explanation: In a const member function the data members are read-only, so x++ inside g() const is an error. Reading x (f), changing a local copy (h) and modifying x in a non-const function (k) are all legal.

questions.questionText: Inside a const member function of class T, what is the type of the this pointer?
options: const T* (a pointer to a const T object)
T* (a pointer to a modifiable T object)
questions.explanation: In a const member function the object is treated as const, so this is a pointer to const T; in a non-const member function it is T*. this is always a pointer, never a reference.
show() is overloaded on const. a is non-const, so the non-const version prints N; b is a const object and r is a const reference (even though it refers to a), so both select the const version: NCC.

options: twice() is const, so this is a const R*, and the non-const function peek() cannot be called through it
A const member function may not read data members, so v must be declared mutable
A const member function can never call another member function
peek() must be declared static before a const function can call it
questions.explanation: Inside a const member function the object is const, and a const object may call only const member functions. Declaring int peek() const fixes it; const functions may read members and may call other const functions.

questions.questionText: Class T has a private data member int x;. Which of these getter definitions inside T fails to compile?
questions.explanation: Inside a const member function x is a const int, and a plain int& cannot bind to a const int because that would let callers modify a const object. Returning const int&, returning a copy, or returning int& from a non-const function are all valid.

questions.questionText: What does the keyword mutable do when applied to a data member?
options: It makes the member shared by all objects of the class
It allows the member to be modified even inside a const member function or in a const object
It makes the member accessible to friend functions only
It prevents the member from ever being changed after construction
questions.explanation: A mutable member is exempt from const: const member functions and const objects may still change it. It is used for caches, counters and similar data that is not part of the object's logical state.

options: Compile error: read() modifies a member of a const object
questions.explanation: hits is mutable, so the const function read() may increment it even on the const object g. s = 7 * 2 = 14 after the first call, the second call makes hits = 2, so the output is 14 2.
In setA the parameter w hides the member, so w = w assigns the parameter to itself and the object is unchanged. setB uses this->w to reach the member, so the stored value stays 4.
Each function returns *this by reference, so every call in the chain works on a itself and runs left to right: 0 + 3 = 3, 3 * 4 = 12, 12 - 2 = 10.
sub(2) changes a to 8 and returns a itself; add(5) changes a to 13 but returns a copy; the final sub(1) acts on that copy (12), which initialises b. So a = 13 and b = 12.
same() compares addresses. r is another name for a, so a.same(r) is true (1); b.same(a) compares &b with &a (0); p points to b, so inside p->same(b) this equals &b (1).

questions.questionText: Which statement about the this pointer is FALSE?
options: Inside obj.f(), this holds the address &obj
return *this; lets a member function return the calling object by reference
this cannot be made to point to a different object inside a member function
Inside a const member function, the non-mutable data members can be modified through this
questions.explanation: In a const member function this has type const T*, so ordinary (non-mutable) members cannot be changed through it. The other statements are true: this equals &obj, *this can be returned by reference for chaining, and this itself cannot be reassigned.
this is the address of the object the function is called on. arr[3].idx(arr) gives &arr[3] - &arr[0] = 3; (p + 2) is arr + 3, so its idx(p) gives (arr + 3) - (arr + 1) = 2.

options: Compile error: a friend function cannot modify private members
questions.explanation: twice() is a friend, so it may change the private x, but it receives W by value and doubles only its copy. a keeps x = 6, so both calls return 6 * 2 = 12.

questions.questionText: Class Rect contains the declaration friend int area(Rect r); and r1 is a Rect object. Which call of area is correct?
questions.explanation: A friend function is not a member of Rect, so it is called like an ordinary function with the object as an argument: area(r1). The member-call forms r1.area() and Rect::area(r1) look for a member that does not exist.

questions.questionText: Class T contains the declaration friend void show(const T &t);. Which definition written outside the class is correct?
options: friend void show(const T &t) { cout << t.v; }
void show(const T &t) const { cout << t.v; }
questions.explanation: A friend is an ordinary non-member function, so it is defined without the T:: prefix and without repeating friend. A trailing const is allowed only on member functions, because it qualifies this.

options: Compile error: a function cannot be a friend of two classes
questions.explanation: One function may be a friend of several classes, so sum() can read both private members: 3 * 10 + 4 = 34.

questions.questionText: The function int sum(const A &, const B &) must read private data of two classes, so both A and B declare it a friend. Class A is defined before class B. Why must the line class B; appear before class A?
options: Without it, B would automatically become a friend of A
A friend function may only be a friend of the class that is defined last
A's friend declaration names B in its parameter list, so B must already be declared (a forward declaration)
It allocates storage for B's objects before A is compiled
questions.explanation: class B; is a forward declaration: it tells the compiler that B is a class so that A's friend declaration can mention const B &. Without it, compiling A fails because B is an unknown type.

options: Compile error: rpm is private to Engine
questions.explanation: friend class Car; lets every member function of Car access Engine's private members. boost() is called twice on the same object (passed by reference): 900 + 100 + 100 = 1100.

options: Only X::readY, because friendship is not mutual
Only Y::readX, because Y is not a member of X
questions.explanation: X declares Y a friend, so Y::readX may read X's private p. Friendship is one-way: Y has not declared X a friend, so X::readY cannot access Y's private q.

F's own member get() may read secret (Line 1), and G may call the inherited public get() (Line 2). Friendship is not inherited, so G's own function direct() has no access to Base's private member (Line 3).

questions.questionText: Class A declares friend class B;, and class B declares friend class C;. Which statement is correct?
options: B can access A's private members, but C cannot
C can access A's private members through B
A can access B's private members
A and C can access each other's private members
questions.explanation: Friendship is granted only by the class being accessed and is neither transitive nor mutual. A trusts B and B trusts C, so B may use A's privates and C may use B's, but C gains nothing in A and A gains nothing in B.

questions.questionText: In which part of a class may a friend declaration be placed?
options: Anywhere in the class body; the access label has no effect on it
Only before the first access specifier
questions.explanation: A friend is not a member, so private, protected and public labels do not apply to its declaration; it grants the same access wherever it appears in the class body.

questions.questionText: Class A, defined before class B, has the public member function void show(B &b);. Inside class B, which declaration makes only this one member function of A (not the whole class A) a friend of B?
questions.explanation: A single member function of another class is befriended with its qualified name: friend void A::show(B &b);. friend class A; would trust every member of A, and friend void show(B &b); befriends an unrelated non-member function.

questions.questionText: What is the main drawback of using friend functions?
options: They weaken encapsulation, because a non-member function gains access to private data
They are always slower because every call is resolved at run time
They cannot take objects of the class as arguments
They can access only the public members of the class
questions.explanation: A friend function breaks the rule that only members touch private data, so every friend widens the set of code that depends on the class internals. Friend calls are ordinary compile-time bound calls and can take objects as arguments.

questions.questionText: Consider these statements: (i) a static member function can be called even when no object of the class exists; (ii) a const member function may modify a data member declared mutable; (iii) a friend function receives a this pointer to the object it is called for; (iv) if class F is a friend of class A, classes derived from F are also friends of A. Which of them are true?
questions.explanation: (i) is true because static functions are called as Class::f(), and (ii) is true because mutable members are exempt from const. (iii) is false since a friend is a non-member with no this, and (iv) is false because friendship is not inherited.

Constructors add 2 and 5 (total = 7). a.twice() adds v = 2 then doubles v to 4; the chained call works on a again (reference), adding 4 and making v = 8; b.twice() adds 5 and makes v = 10. total = 7 + 2 + 4 + 5 = 18.
